citation: The Chicago Democrat. Vol. I, No. 1 (November 26, 1833) through Vol. II, No. 18 (August 26, 1835). Chicago, Ill.: John Calhoun, editor and publisher. Seventy-three issues, OCR-assisted research transcriptions from page scans.
author: John Calhoun, editor and publisher
repository: Page scans supplied to this project by the project owner; transcriptions made for this project under the methodology in chicago/reference/newspapers/Transcriptions/Newspaper_Transcription_Workflow.md. The 1833-11-26 scan set carries a Chicago Historical Society ownership stamp and the pencilled number 51177.
locator: Seventy-three issues, registered one by one with their volume, number, completeness, word count and uncertainty-marker count in chicago/4d/data/research/newspapers/corpus.json. Sixty-six carry a committed .txt beside the .docx in the deposit and are cited there; seven exist as .docx only and are cited at their derived text under chicago/4d/data/research/newspapers/text/. Cite an ISSUE PAGE and COLUMN, never the run and never a whole issue.
rights_note: 1830s imprints, published in the United States before 1929: public domain by expiry, with no renewable interest in the letterpress. The transcriptions are the project owner's own work product, made for this project from scans he supplied. Neither the text nor a quotation from it is encumbered. This does not extend to the page IMAGES, which are held outside the repository and carry whatever the holding repository imposes.
note:
THE TOWN DESCRIBING ITSELF, WEEK BY WEEK, ACROSS THE TWENTY-ONE MONTHS THAT END THREE WEEKS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Everything else this project holds about the town's buildings is retrospective — Andreas 1884 is tier 3 and fifty years late, the chicagology pages are compilations, Wau-Bun is an 1856 memoir. This run is contemporary throughout, and an advertisement is a peculiarly good witness because the advertiser paid for it and his customers had to be able to find him. A Democrat was PRINTED on 1835-07-01, the scene date itself.

THIS RECORD IS THE PUBLICATION. The per-issue record data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json STAYS EXACTLY AS IT IS and is SENIOR to this one for that issue: it was verified by reading the page images directly, at 2.4x-9x, and its readings outrank any transcription-mediated reading of the same issue. Where the two disagree about 1833-11-26, the scan record wins, without argument.

RULING 2, THE OWNER'S, 2026-08-28, RECORDED VERBATIM AND BINDING ON EVERY CLAIM TAKEN FROM THIS PUBLICATION: "Transcription-mediated readings grade `documented`, carrying a flag. The corpus is read through OCR-assisted transcriptions, not the page scans. Every claim taken this way carries `reading: transcription_mediated` and preserves the transcription's own uncertainty brackets. This EXTENDS, and does not overturn, data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json's standard — where a scan exists and is read, the scan remains the authority (it caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'), and a transcription-mediated claim upgrades when a scan read confirms it."

RULING 1, the owner's, same day: "A letter-list name is enough to mint a resident." The post-office letter lists in this run name people by the hundred. A listed name alone makes a resident candidate, not merely a gazetteer entry — and every such claim records `letter_list_only: true`, so the two evidence strengths stay distinguishable forever.

RULING 3, the owner's, same day: "A documented business is BUILT at the scene date unless contradicted." A dissolution, removal or replacement notice is the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town. A business whose last evidence is 1833-1834 is built WITH a survival liberty stated on the record — existence documented, survival to 1835-07-01 assumed — and docs/LIBERTIES.md carries it. Note how much this run asks of that ruling: the population went from 'more than eight hundred souls' in late 1833 to 3,265 by the scene date.

RULING 4, the owner's, 2026-08-28, recorded verbatim: "NOV. 26 is the first issue date I have scanned." It fixes the LOWER BOUND OF THE DEPOSIT, which is a different thing from the lower bound of the publication and is the one the project can actually check things against. Vol. I No. 1 is where the scan holdings start, so no 1833 Democrat scan set precedes it and no argument may reach behind it. This is what settled the undated 'Verified' transcription below, and it is the rule to apply to any future artifact that claims a pre-November-1833 Democrat: the deposit does not hold one.

THE TRAPS THIS PUBLICATION CONTAINS, restated corpus-wide from the per-issue record data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json, which found all three by reading the scan at 2.4x-9x. They are properties of 1830s jobbing printing and of bound volumes, not of one issue, so they apply to every issue in this run.

1. A STOCK CUT IS NOT A PICTURE OF A CHICAGO BUILDING. Nineteenth-century printers kept generic engravings for property, estray and shipping advertisements and struck the same block for any advertiser. No elevation, storey count, roof form or window arrangement may be taken from an engraving in this corpus, ever.

2. AD-COPY DATES ARE NOT ISSUE DATES. An advertisement carries the date its copy was written and ran for weeks or months afterwards. The date at the foot of an advertisement establishes when the trade was being carried on no later than — it does not establish that the advertiser was still there on the issue date, and it is not the issue's own date.

3. A LATER PENCILLED GLOSS IS NOT LETTERPRESS. A modern reader's marginal annotation in a bound volume can read as contemporary corroboration once it is transcribed. The motivating case is exact and it is in this run: an 'S. W.' pencilled in the right margin of the 1833-11-26 advertisement page, level with the Democrat's own imprint, which would silently promote the paper's office from a named JUNCTION to a named CORNER on no evidence at all. Quarantine every annotation that is not letterpress.

4. AND ONE THE CORPUS ADDS. The transcriptions carry the transcriber's own apparatus — headers, editorial-method paragraphs, `[uncertain: ...]`, `[illegible]`, `[missing at edge]` and per-column validation notices. None of it is 1830s type. A citation must name an issue page and column, which is exactly what the apparatus cannot supply.

THE CITATION CONVENTION, and it is a bar, not a suggestion: A CLAIM THAT CANNOT NAME ITS COLUMN CANNOT BE MADE. Cite, in this order — publication; issue date; volume and number as PRINTED; issue page and column, taken from the transcription's own `===== ISSUE PAGE n / PDF PAGE m / COLUMN k OF 6 =====` markers; then the transcription file path and the line range within it. Resolve the path through chicago/4d/data/research/newspapers/corpus.json, which is the register of every issue in this run and the only place the paths are guaranteed current. Preserve the transcription's uncertainty brackets inside any quotation; do not tidy them away. Where the printed volume or number is visibly wrong or repeated, transcribe what is printed and say so — the corpus workflow forbids silently repairing it, and this run repeats a number three times.

WHAT THE RUN IS NOT CONTINUOUS. The deposit holds seventy-three issues, not every issue the Democrat printed. The 1834 validation notes record that no March 11, 1834 issue was supplied and the printed sequence resumes March 18 with No. 16. The gap between 1834-12-24 and 1835-01-21, and again between 1835-01-21 and the 1835-03-25 Extra and 1835-05-20, is a gap in the DEPOSIT and says nothing about whether the paper appeared. An argument from silence across this run is worthless unless the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit — corpus.json is what settles that, and it is why the register exists.

THREE PRINTED IRREGULARITIES, preserved rather than repaired. Vol. II, No. 5 is printed on BOTH 1835-01-21 and 1835-05-20. Vol. II, No. 18 is printed on BOTH 1835-08-19 and 1835-08-26. The 1835-06-04 masthead prints 'Wednesday, June 4, 1835' and June 4, 1835 was a Thursday. Each is visible in the source and each is recorded, not regularised; corpus.json carries the transcriber's own note where one was made. The publication day printed on the masthead changes from Tuesday to Wednesday after the 1834-04-08 issue.

TRANSCRIPTION QUALITY IS NOT UNIFORM AND THE DIFFERENCE IS LARGE. The 1833, 1834 and January-July 1835 batches were reconciled against enlarged page images with a second-reviewer pass. The August 1835 tail and the three `-2` rebuilds are single-pass Tesseract PSM 4/PSM 6 output, and where the two runs cover the same issue — 1835-07-01 and 1835-07-08 — the `-2` text is visibly worse: the reconciled 1835-07-01 renders the same masthead-adjacent heading as 'Altscellang. (From the Western Monthly Magazine. J' — itself imperfect — where the `-2` reads 'faiscella Re / Moe syean Monthly Magasin)', which is not a reading at all. Both are quoted here exactly as they stand in the deposit. 1835-07-15 survives in the deposit ONLY as a `-2` rebuild, so it is the weakest issue in the run and corpus.json says so on the record. Weight a reading by which batch it came from; corpus.json's `status` and `completeness` fields carry it.

THE ONE ARTEFACT WHOSE FILENAME CARRIES NO ISSUE DATE, AND HOW IT WAS SETTLED. Chicago_Democrat_1833_11-16-Verified_Transcription.docx is filed in the 1833 set and is headed a 'best-effort verified reading transcription of the three supplied scan pages' — three images of an 1833 Democrat, which is the scan set the per-issue record describes and was verified against. It is attached to 1833-11-26 as an ALTERNATE witness, at `documented` since 2026-08-28, on RULING 4 above: the deposit's scan holdings begin at Vol. I No. 1, so no earlier 1833 Democrat scan set exists for it to be a reading of. The identification is settled BY ELIMINATION AGAINST THE DEPOSIT, and that is the whole of its warrant. TWO NON-DATES REMAIN ON THE ARTEFACT AND ARE PRESERVED, NOT REPAIRED, per the workflow's rule 2.3: its filename's '11-16', and its own first page's 'Visible date at the top of this supplied page: NOV. 19, 1833'. The Democrat published under neither — Vol. I, No. 1 is November 26 and nothing preceded it — so both are artefacts of the transcription and its naming rather than readings of 1830s type, and neither may be cited as evidence that any such issue existed. NOTE WHAT THE RULING DID NOT DO: nobody re-opened the page images to re-read that masthead. The NOV. 19 line is quarantined and unexplained, not corrected, and a scan read of the first supplied page would still outrank this entry — the standard at the top of this record, that the scan wins without argument, is untouched. 

WHERE THE TEXT IS. The archival transcriptions live at chicago/reference/newspapers/Transcriptions/ and are the owner's deposit, read-only to this project. They were committed to `main` on 2026-08-28 and are NOT on `dev`, where this subtree is developed, so a `dev` checkout cannot open them; T-0275 carries the back-merge, which is not trivial because `main` also carries sixty Finder-duplicate files under site/chicago/4d/data/ that turn this repo's gate red in twenty-three places. The twenty-three issues delivered as .docx only were extracted to chicago/4d/data/research/newspapers/text/ by tools/docx_text.py and ARE committed here, so those are citable on any branch.
access_notes: The .docx transcriptions and the source PDFs are outside the published payload; the PDFs are gitignored on `main` for size and are local to the owner. chicago/4d/data/research/ is research, never payload: tools/publish.sh copies named subdirectories of data/ and this is not one of them, and the gate asserts that nothing under it has reached site/chicago/4d/.
what_it_supplies: that a named trade was being carried on in Chicago in a named week, and often where
self-reported addresses, which are the strongest address evidence this project has: the advertiser was paying, and his customers had to find him
dissolution, removal and replacement notices — the only thing that keeps a documented business out of the 1835 town under the owner's ruling 3
post-office letter lists, naming residents by the hundred (ruling 1: a listed name mints a resident candidate, flagged letter_list_only)
the village and later town ordinances, printed complete — the 7 November 1833 code is the richest single item in the run
arrivals and clearances, which date the piers and the harbour as working structures
public notices that fix a building as a polling place, an auction site or a meeting place on a given day
the paper's own imprint, self-reported: the corner of South Water and Clark streets
twenty-one months of continuous weekly attestation ending three weeks before the scene date, including the issue printed on 1835-07-01
what_it_does_not_supply: any building's form, material, storey count, fenestration or dimensions — an advertisement describes a trade, not a building
the specific corner of any junction it names: 'on the corner of' does not say which of the four
anything at all from an engraving — see trap 1; the cuts are the printer's stock
proof that a business named in 1833 or 1834 still stood on 1835-07-01; that is ruling 3's survival liberty, and it is a liberty
an argument from silence, unless corpus.json shows the issues either side of the silence are both in the deposit
a reading that outranks a scan read of the same passage — see ruling 2 and the C. & I. HARMON case
a citation without an issue page and column
